Other triggers and strategies center on emergency/police/location cues, while no threat, appraisal, or memory content connects to animals or snakes. This makes that item look clinically disconnected rather than merely unusual.

issues.explanation: Compulsive cleaning can occur after sexual assault, but in this profile it is not supported by the other selected items or the formulation. vignette:
Amir is a 54-year-old software engineer who lives alone in a quiet suburb. Two years ago, while working late at a tech campus, he was sexually assaulted by a security guard in a stairwell. The man was wearing a dark uniform; outside, an ambulance siren blared past. No one heard Amir's protests. That precise constellation-the smell of the uniform, the blue light flickering through a small window, the wail of the siren, and the terrifying realization that he was alone with a man in a position of authority-has since become the blueprint of his fear.

In the months that followed, Amir found himself reacting to sirens with a jolt of panic, his heart racing even when the sound came from a distant highway. He began to avoid driving near hospitals or fire stations, and he would take long detours rather than pass the office building where the assault occurred. The sight of a police officer or a military uniform on the street made him turn around and walk in the opposite direction; he could no longer bring himself to attend neighborhood events where uniformed personnel might be present. At work, he requested to move his desk to a corner with only one entrance, and he became visibly tense whenever a colleague-any man-walked too close. He told himself that staying alert was the only way to stay safe; he constantly scanned doorways and parking lots for signs of threat, and he began to feel that the only place he could truly let his guard down was his own locked apartment.

Amir held onto a bitter belief that what had happened was profoundly unjust and that nothing had ever been done about it-he never reported the assault, certain that no one would believe him because the guard was in uniform and he was just a man working late. He also blamed himself, replaying the evening endlessly and thinking, I should have left earlier, I should have been more careful, I should have known better. These thoughts grew heavier each time he avoided a situation: he interpreted his own caution as proof that he was weak and that the world was irreparably dangerous. His avoidance of authorities-he stopped interacting with any person in a uniform or official role, even a mail carrier-only deepened his sense that the system had failed him, and that he could never reclaim a normal emotional life.

The cumulative effect of Amir's hypervigilance was that he often reacted as if he were in immediate danger even when nothing was actually wrong. A sudden car backfire sent him diving for cover; a friendly greeting from a male coworker made his stomach clench. He came to believe that he had lost the ability to feel calm or safe outside his apartment, and that his emotions were permanently broken. The more places he eliminated from his daily route, the more those remaining triggers-sirens, uniformed figures, the mere presence of a man in a quiet space-seemed to loom larger. He stopped going to grocery stores after 6 p.m., stopped meeting friends, and finally stopped going into the office altogether, working remotely from a room whose windows he kept covered.

What finally brought Amir to seek help was a panic attack that hit him in his own living room when an ambulance passed by outside. He realized he could no longer distinguish between real danger and a false alarm, and that his life had shrunk to a single room. He is afraid that therapy will force him to revisit the stairwell, but he is more afraid of spending the rest of his years locked inside, waiting for a siren he cannot escape.
